records.name: Guinea-Bissau
records.summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal — one of few nations in the region never to criminalise it: a 1993 penal code decree omits same-sex offences and a 2014 domestic-violence law protects victims regardless of sexual orientation. No legal gender recognition, no trans framework and no partnership recognition exist, and there is no anti-discrimination protection, so no document or screening pathway for trans travelers is documented.

Enforcement and practical safety dominate: chronic instability (a 2012 coup), a weak national apparatus, documented impunity for security-force abuse (arbitrary killings, torture), documented social hostility and stigma, some violence cases in 2018, no visible LGBT scene, and a poor 34/100 ('Caution') travel-safety score, with no mob-lynching pattern reported for a neighbouring nation.

sources.summary: US State Dept 2012 report on Guinea-Bissau: documents the 2012 coup, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and impunity; notes no criminalisation of same-sex conduct — general security context for visitors.
US State Dept 2011 report: security-force torture, FGM and impunity documented; the LGBT section notes no criminalisation but societal stigma against LGBT people.

Overview of LGBT rights in Guinea-Bissau: same-sex conduct legal since 1993 (penal code decree 4/93 omits same-sex offences); signed the 2008 UN SOGI statement; only married heterosexual couples entitled to larger government housing; domestic-violence law (6/2014) Article 5 protects victims regardless of sexual orientation.
LiquiSearch: LGBT rights in Guinea-Bissau - brief overview page (Wikipedia-derived) noting legal challenges and sections on same-sex activity, relationships, adoption and living conditions.

Mapa.gay country guide for Guinea-Bissau: legal since 1993; no partnership recognition; no trans framework; travel-safety score 34/100 ('Caution'); 9% consider homosexual behaviour morally acceptable — unusually moderate for West Africa; no visible LGBT scene; some violence cases (2018).

records.name: Eswatini
records.summary: Eswatini is dangerous for trans visitors. Common law criminalises same-sex intimacy; trans people have no access to LGR and limited healthcare; the absolute monarchy punishes dissent harshly (sedition laws; activists assassinated, per BTI 2024); LGBT people face documented discrimination. Eswatini Pride has proceeded annually since 2018 under heavy conditions — a small space of visibility.

sources.summary: Country overview updated 12 March 2026: same-sex relations ILLEGAL for men and women throughout Eswatini; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations NOT able to register.
Freedom in the World 2024: Eswatini rated Not Free with an overall score of 17/100 (Political Rights 1/40, Civil Liberties 16/60) - an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space.

BTI 2024 country report: the government denies LGBTQ+ groups the ability to register as organisations, within a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment under an oppressive environment ('Mswati must fall' having become a common protest slogan).

US State Department 2021 report on Eswatini: some traditional, religious and government officials criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In June, LGBTQI+ persons conducted a virtual Pride celebration without incident.
Swazi Media Commentary of December 2018: a church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened - religious-space inclusion documented alongside 'no let-up on discrimination in the kingdom'.

MambaOnline, July 2018: the first eSwatini Pride was declared a 'perfect success' - the inaugural Pride in the kingdom, marking public LGBT visibility in a state where same-sex conduct remains illegal.
MambaOnline, July 2019: Eswatini's registrar of companies refused to register an LGBTI group - the documented administrative blocking of organisational recognition in the kingdom.

records.name: Lesotho
records.summary: Lesotho demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (sodomy common-law crime struck down in 2012); the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho documents failures to prevent violence, harassment and discrimination by state and non-state actors (2024 UPR submission); no LGR; small organised community inside South Africa's geographic envelope.

sources.summary: Joint stakeholder UPR report (Oct 2024) by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho on LGBTQ+ rights in Lesotho: documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level SOGIESC discrimination; same-sex conduct is not criminalised but no protections exist.

ICJ UPR submission (Nov 2024) on Lesotho: highlights LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination among three key concerns (alongside inclusive education for children with disabilities and revocation of NGO lawyers' practising certificates).

SALC + People's Matrix Association + WLSA briefing (Oct 2020): 'Legal Gender Recognition in Lesotho' - analysis of law and policy against international best practice; Matrix is the only known LGBTI organisation in Lesotho; researched by Prof Alex Müller with community consultations.

US State Department 2016 Human Rights Report for Lesotho: documents the LDF mutiny arrests, torture of detainees, the killing of Lt-Gen Mahao, and the LGBT section noting no criminalisation but societal stigma.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Lesotho' (2017): constitutional analysis - section 4(1) 'sex' and 'other status' should include gender identity per the UN Human Rights Committee; no law allows gender-marker changes; a trans person using a non-matching passport could be charged; the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omits gender and sexual orientation.

Lesotho Labour Act 2024 (full text, ILO NATLEX): the new labour law - unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, forced and child labour prohibitions - the current statutory framework for workplace rights.

records.name: Cabo Verde
records.summary: Cabo Verde is workable — Africa's most tolerant jurisdiction alongside South Africa's legal tier. Same-sex relations are legal; employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited; Praia and Mindelo host visible Pride events; the culture is notably relaxed by regional standards. No explicit GI protections and no LGR statute (administrative practice unclear), but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

sources.summary: Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations not criminalised; employment discrimination protection covers sexual orientation (not gender identity); no same-sex union recognition; LGBTIQ orgs register freely; first public Pride 2013 (second African country); 2019–21 polls: 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour; Cabo Verde one of two African UN LGBTI Core Group members, made 2024 UPR anti-discrimination commitments.

Equal Eyes (20 Jul 2018): 2018 Pride Week in Praia — parade plus NGO campaigns (Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, Associação LGBTI de Praia, Associação Arco Iris) petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women engaged.

Observador/Lusa (11 Jul 2017): PM Ulisses Correia e Silva said same-sex marriage is not on the government's agenda, distancing himself from MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro's opposition, after LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020): 'All in this together' - Africans are tolerant on ethnic, religious and national differences but not sexual differences; Cabo Verde, Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe stand out as particularly tolerant countries; tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak even among younger respondents.

Rede Angola interview (22 Jun 2016) with Tchinda Andrade, first publicly self-outed trans woman in Cabo Verde (came out 1997, age 19): describes Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, but reports verbal violence and two physical attacks; civil law blocked her legal change to a female name — no legal gender recognition as of 2016.

records.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
records.summary: São Tomé and Príncipe demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2012; small, peaceful, tourism-growing islands; no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; thin community.

sources.summary: Everything Explained summary: legal since 2012; equal age of consent 18 since 2021 (Law 15/2021, previously 16); no relationship recognition or adoption; Labour Code 2019 Article 16.2 bans workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation; no gender-identity recognition.

Under the Penal Code in force since November 2012 same-sex conduct is legal with an equal age of consent of 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Labour Code (2019) Article 16.2 bans workplace discrimination on sexual orientation, and Penal Code Article 130(2)(d) allows enhanced sentencing for crimes motivated by sexual-orientation hatred. No same-sex marriages, civil unions or partnerships are recognised; a 2016 poll found 46% of Sao Tomeans would not mind an LGBTQ neighbour.

Wikipedia-derived page updated 25 Apr 2026: same-sex conduct legal since the November 2012 Penal Code with equal age of consent 16; no recognition of same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. The page lists no general anti-discrimination protection (the 2019 Labour Code employment ban is not reflected here) and records the country among UN Joint Statement signatories on sexual orientation and gender identity.

records.name: Maldives
records.summary:
Maldives is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp resort/local split. Under the Penal Code and sharia framework, same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 8 years, with 100 lashes available), and gender-nonconforming Maldivians face prosecution and social erasure; activists operate from exile (a 2024 HRC shadow report documents ICCPR violations). BUT: the tourist resort islands operate as a legally distinct world — no LGBT tourist is documented as prosecuted on a resort; the risk concentrates in Malé and local islands.

A resort-only visit is lower-risk than the score suggests; any local-island contact raises it.

sources.summary: HRMI Maldives Summary Report 2024 (second expert survey): human-rights experts most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people — alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers — as at risk of empowerment-rights violations; political participation scores relatively better at 6.4/10 while other civil and political rights score considerably lower.

Erasing 76 Crimes (1 September 2015): police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men (aged 56 and 27) on 29 August for homosexual activity in their private home; the 2014 Penal Code extended criminalisation beyond Muslims to everyone, with death-penalty provisions theoretically in reach; Rainbow Warriors warned tourists could face similar threats.

UN OHCHR compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/2, March 2015) for the Maldives’ second-cycle UPR: records ICCPR/CEDAW/CRC reservations and concerns including sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage; the Human Rights Committee recommended anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and action against stigmatisation of homosexuals.

Maldives national UPR report (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/1, April 2015): the government’s own submission — of 126 first-cycle recommendations it fully accepted 89, partially accepted 11, took note of 6 and rejected 20 with reasons; reports full implementation of 58 and partial implementation of 32 over four years.
